title: Week 4 · Lesson 13: Cardiac Electrophysiology, ECG Interpretation & Arrhythmias — FNP-Level Approach
html:
PHASE 1 · ADVANCED PATHOPHYSIOLOGY + CLINICAL REASONING

Week 4 — Lesson 13: Cardiac Electrophysiology, ECG Interpretation & Arrhythmias

FNP-level goal

Use a repeatable ECG framework to connect cardiac electrical mechanisms with perfusion, distinguish common rhythm patterns, identify dangerous bradyarrhythmias and ventricular rhythms, select an appropriate initial evaluation, and decide when a patient needs emergency care rather than outpatient monitoring.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain how impulses arise and move through the SA node, atria, AV node, His-Purkinje system, and ventricles.
  • Confirm paper calibration and calculate rate, rhythm regularity, PR interval, QRS duration, and QT/QTc before accepting a machine interpretation.
  • Recognize the representative features of sinus rhythm, atrial fibrillation, regular narrow-complex SVT, first-degree AV block, ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, and torsades de pointes.
  • Differentiate narrow- from wide-complex tachycardia and organized from disorganized electrical activity.
  • Connect AF to thromboembolism, conduction disease to syncope, myocardial scar to VT, and electrolyte or medication effects to QT-related risk.
  • Choose targeted diagnostics and ambulatory monitoring based on the clinical question and symptom frequency.
  • Recognize hemodynamic instability and activate emergency care before pursuing detailed rhythm classification.
How to use the ECG figures: These are simplified teaching strips created for pattern recognition. They are not patient tracings, are not diagnostic, and are not substitutes for a calibrated 12-lead ECG interpreted in clinical context.

Part 1 — Electrical conduction becomes mechanical output

The usual electrical pathway is SA node → atria → AV node → His bundle → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibers → ventricles. The SA node normally initiates the impulse. Atrial depolarization corresponds primarily to the P wave; ventricular depolarization to the QRS complex; and ventricular repolarization to the T wave.

The AV node introduces a brief delay so atrial contraction can support ventricular filling before the ventricles activate. Rapid conduction through the His-Purkinje network then coordinates ventricular contraction. Electrical timing matters because an impulse that is too slow, too fast, blocked, or disorganized may reduce stroke volume and cardiac output even when the myocardium itself is structurally intact.

Never equate electrical activity with adequate circulation. A monitor can display an organized rhythm while the patient has no effective pulse, and a patient can have an abnormal ECG while maintaining stable perfusion. The tracing and the patient must be assessed together.

Part 2 — What an ECG can and cannot tell you

A 12-lead ECG is a brief surface recording of cardiac electrical activity from multiple viewpoints. It can reveal rhythm, rate, conduction delay, chamber-related patterns, ischemic changes, prior infarction clues, pre-excitation, and medication or electrolyte effects. It does not directly measure cardiac output, coronary anatomy, valve severity, ejection fraction, or the cause of every symptom.

A normal resting ECG also does not exclude a paroxysmal arrhythmia. If palpitations or syncope occurred yesterday and the rhythm has normalized, the office ECG may be normal. The FNP must decide whether the next step is reassurance, targeted laboratory testing, echocardiography, ambulatory rhythm monitoring, cardiology consultation, or emergency evaluation.

Part 3 — Verify the tracing before interpreting it

Before naming a rhythm, confirm patient identity, symptoms at the time of acquisition, lead placement, artifact, and calibration. Standard recording is commonly 25 mm/second and 10 mm/mV. At 25 mm/second, one small horizontal box is 0.04 second and one large box is 0.20 second. Five large boxes equal one second.

Look for a calibration mark and check whether the baseline is stable. Tremor, shivering, loose electrodes, limb movement, electrical interference, and lead reversal can simulate arrhythmia or alter morphology. If the tracing does not fit the pulse or clinical picture, verify the patient and repeat a technically adequate ECG before anchoring on the automated label.

Part 4 — The FNP six-step rhythm approach

  1. Stability: Is there hypotension, acutely altered mental status, shock, ischemic chest discomfort, acute heart failure, severe dyspnea, syncope, or collapse?
  2. Rate: Fast, slow, or within the expected range for the situation?
  3. Regularity: Regular, regularly irregular, or irregularly irregular?
  4. Atrial activity: Are P waves present? Do they look alike? Is one P associated with each QRS?
  5. Intervals: Is the PR constant and plausible? Is the QRS narrow or wide? Is the QT/QTc concerning?
  6. Context: Symptoms, medications, electrolytes, ischemia, structural disease, thyroid status, infection, substances, and prior tracings.

Stability comes first because the same rhythm label can have very different consequences. A rate of 170/min in a stable young adult is not managed with the same urgency as a rate of 170/min accompanied by BP 76/44, confusion, pulmonary edema, or ischemic chest pain.

Part 5 — Normal sinus rhythm

A sinus rhythm begins in the SA node. Typical features include regular P waves with a consistent morphology, one P wave before each QRS, a consistent PR interval, and an organized ventricular response. A conventional resting sinus rate is often described as 60–100/min, but the rate must still be interpreted in context.

“Sinus” describes the impulse origin, not overall health. Sinus tachycardia may be an appropriate response to fever, hypovolemia, pain, anemia, hypoxemia, sepsis, pulmonary embolism, or hyperthyroidism. Sinus bradycardia may be physiologic in an athlete or pathologic in medication toxicity, inferior ischemia, hypothermia, metabolic disease, or conduction-system dysfunction.

Part 6 — Calculating rate instead of trusting the monitor

For a regular rhythm recorded at 25 mm/second, divide 300 by the number of large boxes between consecutive R waves. A more precise option is 1500 divided by the number of small boxes. For an irregular rhythm, count QRS complexes in a 6-second strip and multiply by 10 for an approximate rate.

Rate calculations are estimates when the rhythm is highly irregular or the strip is short. Always compare the electrical rate with a palpated pulse because a pulse deficit can occur when some ventricular contractions do not generate effective peripheral pulses.

Part 7 — PR, QRS, and QT/QTc

  • PR interval: atrial depolarization through AV conduction. A usual adult range is approximately 0.12–0.20 second. A PR interval greater than 0.20 second with 1:1 conduction is first-degree AV delay/block.
  • QRS duration: ventricular depolarization. A QRS of 0.12 second or more is considered wide in acute rhythm algorithms and broadens the differential to ventricular origin, bundle-branch aberrancy, pre-excitation, pacing, or metabolic/toxic causes.
  • QT interval: ventricular depolarization plus repolarization. Because QT varies with rate, clinicians use a corrected QT, or QTc. Automated QTc values require visual review, especially with irregular rhythms, broad QRS complexes, merged T/U waves, or artifact.

A prolonged QT is a risk marker, not a rhythm diagnosis. Risk rises with the degree of prolongation and with multiple contributors such as hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, bradycardia, congenital long-QT syndromes, interacting QT-prolonging drugs, or acute illness.

Part 8 — Bradycardia: treat the patient, then define the mechanism

Bradycardia becomes clinically important when the rate is inadequate for the patient and causes cardiopulmonary compromise. Concerning features include hypotension, acutely altered mentation, shock, ischemic discomfort, acute heart failure, severe weakness, presyncope, or syncope. A fit asymptomatic adult with a resting rate of 52/min and an older adult taking AV-nodal blockers with a rate of 34/min and dizziness are not equivalent.

Review beta blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers, digoxin, antiarrhythmics, sedatives, and recent medication changes. Search for ischemia, hypoxia, hypothermia, hypothyroidism, infection, potassium disturbance, sleep apnea, and intrinsic sinus-node or conduction disease. Symptomatic bradycardia requires timely monitoring and emergency management according to current protocols; do not delay disposition while trying to name every conduction subtype.

Part 9 — AV block patterns

  • First-degree AV block: every P conducts, but PR is consistently longer than 0.20 second. This is more accurately AV delay because no impulse is actually dropped.
  • Second-degree Mobitz I: PR progressively lengthens until a P wave is not followed by a QRS, then the cycle resets. The level is often nodal, but context matters.
  • Second-degree Mobitz II: conducted beats have a relatively constant PR, but some P waves abruptly fail to conduct. This suggests more serious His-Purkinje disease and can progress to complete block.
  • Third-degree AV block: atria and ventricles depolarize independently. P waves and QRS complexes have no fixed relationship; the escape rhythm may be slow and unreliable.

Do not confuse a blocked premature atrial beat with AV block, and do not reassure solely because the ventricular rate is currently adequate. New Mobitz II, high-grade AV block, or complete heart block—especially with symptoms, wide QRS escape, ischemia, or structural disease—requires urgent emergency and cardiology evaluation.

Part 10 — Tachycardia: narrow or wide, regular or irregular

After stability, QRS width and regularity rapidly narrow the differential:

  • Regular narrow: sinus tachycardia, AVNRT/AVRT, atrial tachycardia, or atrial flutter with fixed conduction.
  • Irregular narrow: atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter with variable conduction, or multifocal atrial tachycardia.
  • Regular wide: VT, SVT with aberrancy, pre-excited tachycardia, or paced rhythm.
  • Irregular wide: AF with aberrancy, pre-excited AF, polymorphic VT, or frequent ventricular ectopy.

Wide-complex tachycardia in an older adult with prior MI or structural heart disease should be treated as VT until expert evaluation proves otherwise. Some AV-nodal blocking medications can be dangerous in pre-excited rhythms; avoid reflex treatment of an uncertain wide-complex tachycardia from an outpatient setting.

Part 11 — Regular narrow-complex SVT and reentry

SVT is a broad category of rapid rhythms arising above the ventricles. AV nodal reentrant tachycardia and AV reentrant tachycardia often start and stop abruptly. Patients may describe a sudden switch-like onset, rapid regular pounding, neck pulsations, lightheadedness, dyspnea, anxiety, or chest pressure.

Reentry occurs when an impulse repeatedly circulates through pathways with different conduction and refractory properties. The loop re-excites tissue and sustains tachycardia. In a stable patient with a regular narrow rhythm, vagal maneuvers and adenosine may be used in an appropriately monitored clinical setting under current protocol. Persistent symptoms, diagnostic uncertainty, structural heart disease, or instability should prompt escalation rather than an unsupervised office intervention.

Do not assume every rate near 150/min is SVT. Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction commonly produces a regular ventricular rate near 150/min, while severe physiologic stress can produce sinus tachycardia. Search for atrial activity, compare prior ECGs, and treat the underlying illness when sinus tachycardia is the response rather than the primary disorder.

Part 12 — Atrial fibrillation: recognize and confirm

In AF, multiple disorganized atrial wavefronts replace coordinated atrial depolarization. The atria do not contract effectively, and AV-node conduction produces an irregularly irregular ventricular response. The ECG diagnosis requires visual confirmation; pulse irregularity or a smartwatch alert is a clue, not sufficient evidence by itself.

Loss of atrial contraction reduces ventricular filling, especially in older adults, HFpEF, mitral stenosis, or other stiff-ventricle states. A rapid ventricular response further shortens diastole and can trigger ischemia, hypotension, or pulmonary congestion. Conversely, AF with a controlled rate can still carry thromboembolic risk.

Part 13 — The complete AF assessment

After recognizing AF, ask five separate questions:

  1. Is the patient stable? Instability attributable to AF changes immediate management.
  2. What is the ventricular rate and symptom burden? Rate control, rhythm strategy, and disposition depend on context.
  3. When did it begin? Duration and certainty of onset affect cardioversion and anticoagulation planning.
  4. What triggered or sustains it? Infection, hyperthyroidism, alcohol, sleep apnea, pulmonary disease, electrolyte disturbance, ischemia, heart failure, and medications matter.
  5. What is the stroke and bleeding risk? Use current guideline-based validated risk assessment and shared decision-making rather than the rhythm label alone.

Ineffective atrial contraction promotes stasis, particularly in the left atrial appendage. Thrombus can embolize and cause ischemic stroke. Anticoagulation choice is also shaped by kidney function, drug interactions, bleeding history, adherence, mechanical valves, and moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis. This is a longitudinal clinical decision, not a one-time checkbox.

Part 14 — Atrial flutter and multifocal atrial tachycardia

Atrial flutter is an organized macro-reentrant atrial rhythm, often with flutter waves and a predictable conduction ratio. With 2:1 AV conduction, the ventricular rhythm may be regular near 150/min and mistaken for SVT or sinus tachycardia. Variable conduction can make it irregular.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia is an irregular narrow-complex tachycardia with at least three distinct P-wave morphologies and varying PR intervals. It is often associated with pulmonary disease, hypoxemia, or acute systemic illness. The key clinical move is to treat the underlying driver, not merely the monitor rate.

Part 15 — Premature beats and ectopy

A premature atrial contraction originates outside the SA node and usually produces an early abnormal P wave followed by a narrow QRS. A premature ventricular contraction originates in ventricular myocardium; depolarization spreads cell-to-cell rather than through the normal His-Purkinje network, producing an early wide QRS without a preceding normal P wave.

Occasional PVCs can occur in healthy people. Risk interpretation changes with exertional symptoms, syncope, family history of sudden death, frequent or multifocal PVCs, runs of nonsustained VT, prior MI, cardiomyopathy, stimulant exposure, or electrolyte abnormality. Quantify burden with appropriate monitoring when clinically indicated and evaluate for structural disease when the context suggests it.

Part 16 — Ventricular tachycardia

VT arises from ventricular myocardium and commonly produces a wide-complex rhythm. Monomorphic VT has a consistent QRS morphology and often reflects scar-related reentry after MI or in cardiomyopathy. Polymorphic VT changes morphology and raises different concerns, including acute ischemia and long-QT–associated torsades.

Fast ventricular activation reduces filling time and may produce inefficient contraction, hypotension, syncope, shock, or cardiac arrest. A pulse can be present or absent. The first clinical questions are therefore: Does the patient have a pulse, and is there cardiopulmonary compromise? Do not spend critical minutes measuring every interval in an unstable patient.

Part 17 — Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless VT

VF produces no coordinated ventricular contraction, so effective cardiac output is absent. Pulseless VT is also a shockable cardiac-arrest rhythm. If a patient collapses, is unresponsive, is not breathing normally, and has no pulse, activate emergency response, begin high-quality CPR, and use an AED/defibrillator according to current resuscitation protocol.

Artifact can resemble VF. The patient resolves the uncertainty: someone who is awake, talking, and has a stable palpable pulse is not in true ventricular fibrillation. Check leads and obtain a clean tracing, but never delay resuscitation when the patient is pulseless.

Part 18 — Prolonged QT and torsades de pointes

Torsades de pointes is a polymorphic VT associated with a prolonged QT interval. The complexes change axis and amplitude, creating a waxing-and-waning appearance. It may terminate spontaneously, recur, cause syncope, or deteriorate into VF.

Review every medication and interaction when QT is prolonged. Common contributors include hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, bradycardia, congenital long-QT syndromes, antiarrhythmics, selected antibiotics, antipsychotics, antidepressants, antiemetics, methadone, and acute systemic illness. Correct reversible causes and follow emergency protocols. Sustained polymorphic VT requires immediate emergency treatment; magnesium is specifically considered for recurrent torsades associated with long QT, not as routine therapy for every polymorphic VT.

Part 19 — Potassium, magnesium, and toxic-metabolic clues

Potassium strongly influences resting membrane potential and repolarization. Hyperkalemia may produce tall peaked T waves, PR prolongation, loss of visible P waves, QRS widening, bradyarrhythmia, sine-wave morphology, VF, or asystole. The sequence is variable, and a normal-appearing ECG does not safely exclude dangerous hyperkalemia.

Hypokalemia can cause T-wave flattening, ST depression, prominent U waves, ventricular ectopy, and increased risk of QT-related arrhythmia, especially with hypomagnesemia or QT-prolonging medications. Check kidney function, diuretic use, RAAS-blocking therapy, vomiting/diarrhea, DKA treatment, supplements, and recent medication changes.

Sodium-channel blocker toxicity, digoxin effect/toxicity, hypothermia, hypoglycemia, hypoxemia, acid-base disturbance, and ischemia can also alter rate, conduction, or repolarization. The ECG can be the first clue to a systemic emergency.

Part 20 — Ischemia and structural heart disease change the risk

Acute ischemia alters membrane potentials and creates electrical heterogeneity, predisposing to ventricular arrhythmias. Prior infarction leaves scar that can support reentry. Cardiomyopathy, ventricular hypertrophy, valve disease, congenital heart disease, and heart failure all change pretest probability and disposition.

Palpitations plus ongoing pressure-like chest discomfort, diaphoresis, dyspnea, syncope, or ischemic ECG changes need urgent emergency assessment. Do not label symptoms as anxiety or benign ectopy before considering acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, severe anemia, thyrotoxicosis, infection, or other high-risk causes.

Part 21 — Artifact, computer interpretation, and wearable devices

Computer-generated ECG interpretations are useful screening aids but can mislabel AF, infarction, conduction disease, or QT prolongation. Review the actual tracing, compare prior ECGs, and obtain expert over-read when the finding changes management.

Consumer watches and handheld single-lead devices can capture useful rhythm information, especially during symptoms. They may detect an irregular rhythm or produce a tracing that supports AF, but false positives occur with motion, ectopy, poor contact, or artifact. A notification should lead to clinical confirmation rather than automatic diagnosis or anticoagulation.

Part 22 — Focused history and examination

Clarify onset, offset, duration, frequency, triggers, exertional relationship, abrupt versus gradual onset, regular versus irregular sensation, and associated chest discomfort, dyspnea, presyncope, syncope, neurologic symptoms, fever, bleeding, or volume loss. Ask about caffeine/energy products, alcohol, nicotine, decongestants, stimulants, illicit substances, and supplement use.

Review cardiac history, HF, prior MI, valve disease, thyroid disease, lung disease, sleep apnea, kidney disease, pregnancy possibility, family history of cardiomyopathy or sudden death, and every prescription/OTC medication. On examination, assess airway/breathing, mental status, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, pulse regularity and deficit, volume status, murmurs, HF signs, perfusion, and focal neurologic findings.

Part 23 — Targeted diagnostic strategy

  • 12-lead ECG: document rhythm, intervals, QRS width, ischemic changes, pre-excitation, and comparison with prior tracings.
  • Labs selected by presentation: electrolytes, magnesium, renal function, glucose, CBC, thyroid studies, pregnancy testing when relevant, toxicology or drug levels when indicated, and cardiac biomarkers when ischemia or myocardial injury is suspected.
  • Echocardiography: consider when structural disease, HF, valve disease, cardiomyopathy, significant arrhythmia, or abnormal examination is suspected.
  • Ambulatory monitoring: match device duration to symptom frequency and severity. A 24–48 hour Holter is more useful for daily symptoms; longer patch/event monitoring improves yield when symptoms are less frequent. Very infrequent concerning syncope may require specialist consideration of an implantable monitor.
  • Referral: cardiology/electrophysiology for documented significant arrhythmia, high-grade conduction disease, pre-excitation, recurrent symptomatic SVT, complex ventricular ectopy, unexplained syncope, or uncertain high-risk tracings.

Testing should answer a clinical question. A broad untargeted lab panel or a short monitor for symptoms occurring once every three months may generate cost without capturing the event.

Part 24 — Primary care, expedited referral, or emergency care?

Potentially appropriate for structured outpatient evaluation

  • Stable vitals and perfusion.
  • No syncope, ischemic discomfort, acute HF, or severe dyspnea.
  • Brief self-limited palpitations with a low-risk history and examination.
  • A clear plan for ECG, targeted labs, symptom-rhythm correlation, follow-up, and return precautions.

Needs expedited cardiology evaluation

  • New documented AF or recurrent symptomatic SVT.
  • Frequent ventricular ectopy, nonsustained VT, or abnormal conduction in structural heart disease.
  • Unexplained presyncope/syncope, exertional symptoms, or family history of sudden death.
  • Possible high-grade AV block, pre-excitation, marked QT prolongation, or an abnormal ECG that changes risk.

Emergency evaluation

  • Hypotension, acutely altered mental status, shock, ischemic chest discomfort, or acute heart failure attributable to the rhythm.
  • Sustained wide-complex tachycardia, polymorphic VT, severe symptomatic bradycardia, high-grade block with compromise, or severe electrolyte disturbance with ECG changes.
  • Syncope with ongoing abnormal vital signs, exertional/supine event plus high-risk features, or suspected acute ischemia.
  • Collapse, absent normal breathing, or no pulse: activate emergency response, CPR, and AED/defibrillation.

Case 1 — New AF with rapid ventricular response

A 76-year-old reports 24 hours of palpitations and fatigue. Pulse is 132/min and irregular; BP is 118/72; oxygen saturation is 96%; ECG shows no consistent P waves and irregularly irregular narrow QRS complexes. She has no chest pain, pulmonary edema, hypotension, or neurologic deficit.

Reasoning: AF is likely and she appears currently stable, but the work is not finished. Confirm duration, assess HF and ischemic symptoms, review medications and alcohol, obtain targeted electrolytes/renal and thyroid testing, evaluate stroke and bleeding risk, and arrange timely management. If pulmonary edema, hypotension, ischemic discomfort, or altered mentation develops, the pathway changes to emergency rhythm management.

Case 2 — Regular narrow tachycardia

A 34-year-old develops abrupt palpitations while seated. HR is 188/min, regular; QRS is narrow; BP is 126/78; mentation and perfusion are normal. There is no chest pain or HF.

Reasoning: Reentry-related SVT is plausible. Confirm rhythm with 12-lead ECG if it does not delay care. In an appropriately equipped setting, regular narrow-complex tachycardia may be approached with monitored vagal maneuvers and protocol-based therapy. A gradual-onset tachycardia with fever and dehydration would instead suggest sinus tachycardia and require treatment of the driver.

Case 3 — Unstable wide-complex tachycardia

A 68-year-old with prior MI develops sudden dizziness and chest pressure. BP is 76/44; monitor shows a regular wide-complex rhythm at 180/min.

Reasoning: Scar-related VT is highly concerning. Hypotension and ischemic discomfort show cardiopulmonary compromise. Activate emergency response and follow the synchronized-cardioversion pathway for unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse. Detailed outpatient differential diagnosis must not delay treatment.

Case 4 — Medication-associated symptomatic bradycardia

An 82-year-old taking metoprolol and diltiazem presents with weakness and near-syncope. HR is 36/min, BP is 88/54, and ECG shows marked bradycardia.

Reasoning: AV-nodal medication effect or interaction is possible, but ischemia, electrolyte disturbance, and intrinsic conduction disease remain in the differential. Hypotension and presyncope make this an emergency. Medication reconciliation is essential, but simply telling the patient to skip a dose and go home is unsafe.

Case 5 — Intermittent syncope and a normal office ECG

A 70-year-old has two sudden syncopal episodes without prodrome. Today the ECG is normal. He has a history of structural heart disease.

Reasoning: A normal snapshot does not exclude intermittent high-grade block or tachyarrhythmia. Sudden syncope without prodrome plus structural disease is high risk. Disposition should reflect that risk, and monitoring duration must match event frequency; a routine 24-hour Holter may be inadequate if events are months apart.

Case 6 — QT risk stack

A patient taking a QT-prolonging antiemetic and antibiotic develops vomiting, potassium 2.9 mEq/L, magnesium deficiency, palpitations, and a markedly prolonged QTc.

Reasoning: Multiple acquired risk factors are stacking: drug interaction, electrolyte loss, and prolonged repolarization. Stop and review offending medications, urgently correct reversible factors in an appropriate monitored setting, and recognize syncope or polymorphic VT as an emergency.

Case 7 — Smartwatch AF notification

A 59-year-old has three smartwatch alerts for possible AF but feels well. The pulse is intermittently irregular; the office ECG shows sinus rhythm with occasional premature beats.

Reasoning: Do not diagnose AF from the alert alone, but do not dismiss it. Review the saved strips if available, assess stroke/structural risk and symptoms, and select ambulatory monitoring likely to capture an event. Anticoagulation should not begin solely because an algorithm displayed “possible AF.”

Case 8 — CKD, weakness, and an electrical emergency

A patient with advanced CKD reports weakness. Potassium is 7.0 mEq/L, and ECG shows progressive conduction abnormalities.

Reasoning: Reduced renal potassium excretion can destabilize membrane electrophysiology and cause fatal arrhythmia. This needs emergency treatment and monitoring. Conversely, absence of classic peaked T waves would not make a potassium of 7.0 safe.

FNP High-Yield Workflow

  1. Look at the patient before the tracing: pulse, perfusion, BP, mentation, breathing, pain, and HF signs.
  2. Confirm calibration and exclude artifact or lead error.
  3. Determine rate and regularity.
  4. Identify P waves and the P–QRS relationship.
  5. Measure PR and QRS; inspect QT/QTc and ST-T morphology.
  6. Classify the pattern without overclaiming certainty.
  7. Search for reversible and dangerous causes.
  8. Match testing and monitoring to the clinical question.
  9. Choose disposition: outpatient plan, expedited cardiology, or emergency care.
  10. Document return precautions and close the follow-up loop.

High-Yield Summary

Normal pathway: SA → AV → His → bundle branches → Purkinje.
ECG basics: P = atrial depolarization; QRS = ventricular depolarization; T = ventricular repolarization.
Calibration: at 25 mm/second, one small box = 0.04 second and one large box = 0.20 second.
AF: no consistent P waves + irregularly irregular rhythm; confirm visually and assess stability, duration, triggers, structure, and stroke risk.
Regular narrow tachycardia: consider SVT, flutter with fixed conduction, atrial tachycardia, and sinus tachycardia.
Wide tachycardia: consider VT first in structural heart disease; instability takes priority over perfect classification.
AV block: distinguish prolonged conduction from dropped beats and AV dissociation.
VT/VF: determine pulse and perfusion immediately.
Long QT: look for medications, low potassium/magnesium, bradycardia, congenital risk, and torsades.
Monitoring: choose duration based on symptom frequency; a normal office ECG does not exclude an intermittent arrhythmia.

Evidence Anchors & Current Practice References

  • 2025 American Heart Association Guidelines — Adult Advanced Life Support
  • 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation
  • 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay
  • 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Syncope Guideline — Executive Summary
  • AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for ECG Standardization and Interpretation

Educational scope: Use current emergency protocols, local policy, specialist input, and patient-specific judgment. This lesson does not replace ACLS training, ECG over-read, or individualized medical care.
